title: Web
text: The published files can be used directly by web apps: the site serves them with cross-origin access allowed, and supports HTTP range requests (used by GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf readers). Everything on this page runs in your browser.

title: QGIS
text:
In QGIS, Layer ▸ Add Layer ▸ Add Vector Layer…, choose Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc., and enter a URL:
https://australianantarcticdivision.github.io/measoshapes/data/v06/measo_regions06.fgb
Use FlatGeobuf (.fgb), which every recent QGIS can read. GeoParquet (.parquet) works if your QGIS build includes the GDAL Parquet driver (check Settings ▸ Options ▸ GDAL ▸ Vector Drivers). You can also download a file from the Data page and drag it onto the map.
Which file:

measo_regions06.fgb: polar equal area, for maps of the Southern Ocean and areas.
measo_regions06_epsg_3031.fgb: polar stereographic (EPSG:3031), to match Quantarctica and other EPSG:3031 data.
measo_regions06_ll.fgb: longitude/latitude.

QGIS reprojects layers on the fly, so any of them can be shown in a project in another projection.

title: QGIS
text:
Colours and labels
Download the style measo_regions06.qml, then in the layer’s Properties ▸ Symbology, choose Style ▸ Load Style… and select the file. The regions are categorized by name with the fill colours and legend labels such as “Antarctic Atlantic (AOA)”; the T regions (outside MEASO) are outlined only.
Alternatively, use the fill column directly: in Symbology, set the fill colour to Data defined override ▸ Edit… with the expression
coalesce("fill", '#00000000')
and use label for labels.

title: QGIS
text:
From the Python console
base = "https://australianantarcticdivision.github.io/measoshapes/data/v06"
layer = iface.addVectorLayer(f"/vsicurl/{base}/measo_regions06.fgb", "MEASO regions", "ogr")

import urllib.request, tempfile, os
qml = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "measo_regions06.qml")
urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{base}/measo_regions06.qml", qml)
layer.loadNamedStyle(qml)
layer.triggerRepaint()

title: News
text:
measoshapes 0.0.06

Release “06” adds measo_regions06 (with _ll, _coastline and _ll_coastline forms) and measo_names06. The boundaries are those of version 05. In version 06:

one row per region (20 rows): the WestPacific regions, split at the anti-meridian in 05, are one feature each
name, label, sector, zone, and fill are on the features; label is the full name, zone then sector, e.g. “Antarctic Atlantic”
fill is the colour of each region in the MEASO Summary for Policymakers (Constable et al. 2023, Figure 5): each sector has its own hue, light to dark from the Antarctic to the Northern zone
a current crs

Version 05 is kept as it was released. Its colours have sectors sharing palettes (WestPacific with Atlantic, EastPacific with CentralIndian), and the first WPA row of measo_names has a fill that doesn’t match the second (an error, kept as released).
Files for version 06 in ‘inst/extdata’: GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf in polar LAEA, longitude/latitude and EPSG:3031, GeoJSON in longitude/latitude, and a QGIS style. The version 05 geopackages are unchanged.
Added references to the MEASO Summary for Policymakers, McCormack et al. (2021), and earlier MEASO documents (citation("measoshapes"), ?measo_regions06).
Known: the MEASO Summary for Policymakers describes the Northern zone as “no further north than 40°S”; in the Atlantic (9°W to 10°E) the Northern region (AON) reaches 38.3°S.

title: Illustrations
text: All figures on this page are made in R from the published files and the package data sets; expand “Code” to see how.

title: Illustrations
text:
Colours
The colours of the MEASO Summary for Policymakers (Figure 5); see Definition.

Code
colour_table <- function(x) {
cell <- function(name, fill) {
  if (is.na(fill)) return(sprintf("<td>%s</td>", name))
  rgb <- col2rgb(fill)
  fg <- if (sum(rgb * c(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) > 140) "black" else "white"
  sprintf('<td style="background:%s;color:%s">%s<br><code style="background:none;color:%s">%s</code></td>',
          substr(fill, 1, 7), fg, name, fg, substr(fill, 1, 7))
}
zones <- c("Antarctic", "Subantarctic", "Northern", NA)
rows <- vapply(unique(x$sector), function(s) {
  d <- x[x$sector == s, ]
  cells <- vapply(zones, function(z) {
    i <- which(if (is.na(z)) is.na(d$zone) else d$zone %in% z)
    cell(d$name[i], d$fill[i])
  }, "")
  sprintf("<tr><th>%s</th>%s</tr>", s, paste(cells, collapse = ""))
}, "")
cat('<table class="table" style="text-align:center">',
    "<tr><th></th><th>Antarctic</th><th>Subantarctic</th><th>Northern</th><th>(outside)</th></tr>",
    rows, "</table>", sep = "\n")
}
colour_table(x)

title: Definition
text:
Note



This page describes version 06. Its boundaries are those of version 05, built by data-raw/munge-sectors05.R; version 06 is made from version 05 by data-raw/munge-sectors06.R (see History).

title: Definition
text:
Sectors and zones
Each region is a combination of a sector and a zone. These are the MEASO assessment areas of the MEASO Summary for Policymakers (Constable et al. 2023, Figure 5), adapted from McCormack et al. (2021); see References.

Sectors (west to east from the Pacific): West Pacific, East Pacific, Atlantic, Central Indian, East Indian. Their boundaries are near 125°W, the Drake Passage and Antarctic Peninsula, 30°E, 115°E, and 158–170°E (with a dog-leg at the Ross Sea).
Zones (south to north): Antarctic (south of the Southern Antarctic Circumpolar Current Front, SACCF), Subantarctic (SACCF to the Subantarctic Front, SAF), Northern (SAF to the Subtropical Front, STF).
North of the STF, to 30°S, each sector has a T region (temperate). These are not part of MEASO; they have no zone and no colour, and exist so that every location in the domain falls in exactly one region.

Region names are the sector code followed by the zone code, e.g. EIS is East Indian Subantarctic.

title: Definition
text:
Construction
The regions are not drawn as polygons. They are built from lines:

sector boundary lines, extended from 85°S to 30°S,
the three fronts, as simplified, stair-stepped lines around the whole Southern Ocean,
the edges of the domain: 85°S, 30°S, and the anti-meridian.

The lines are noded together and polygonized (sf::st_polygonize()), very small slivers are dropped, and the polygons are named. Because every polygon comes from the same set of lines, the regions share their boundaries exactly: there are no gaps or overlaps, and together they cover the domain.


Code
## sector lines, as in data-raw/munge-sectors05.R
minlat <- -85; maxlat <- -30
s <- data.frame(lon = c(-125, -125,  -70, -64.5, -60, -55.054477039271191, -63.799776827053591, -63.799776827053591,
                        30, 30,   115, 115,   158, 158, 170, 170, 170),
                lat = c(minlat, maxlat,  minlat, -66, -64, -63.260598133971456, -54.721070105901589, maxlat,
                        minlat, maxlat,   minlat, maxlat,   minlat, -75, -71.60, -47.50, maxlat),
                id = c(1, 1, rep(2, 6), 3, 3, 4, 4, rep(5, 5)))
sectors <- st_sfc(lapply(split(s, s$id), \(d) st_linestring(cbind(d$lon, d$lat))))
load("../data-raw/zones.Rdata")
fronts <- st_geometry(zones)
domain <- st_sfc(st_linestring(cbind(c(-180, 180, 180, -180, -180), c(minlat, minlat, maxlat, maxlat, minlat))))

op <- par(mfrow = c(4, 1), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 0.5))
lim <- list(xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(minlat, maxlat))
plot(domain, col = "grey80", xlim = lim$xlim, ylim = lim$ylim, main = "(a) sectors")
plot(sectors, add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
plot(domain, col = "grey80", main = "(b) fronts")
fcol <- c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3")
plot(fronts, add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = fcol)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("SACCF", "SAF", "STF"), col = fcol, lwd = 2, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE)
plot(domain, lwd = 2, main = "(c) all lines")
plot(sectors, add = TRUE); plot(fronts, add = TRUE)
ll <- st_set_crs(measo_regions06_ll, NA)  ## planar, as in (a)-(c)
plot(st_geometry(ll), col = ifelse(is.na(ll$fill), "grey95", ll$fill),
     border = "grey40", main = "(d) regions")
par(op)








Figure 1: Construction in longitude/latitude: (a) sector lines, (b) fronts (SACCF, SAF, STF), (c) all lines with the domain, (d) the resulting regions.






Boundaries are straight in longitude/latitude
The regions are defined in longitude/latitude as a plane: each boundary segment is a straight line in longitude and latitude. Most segments run along a parallel or a meridian (the fronts are stair-stepped), so “straight in longitude/latitude” means a boundary at 30°S follows the 30°S parallel. This is the same interpretation as GeoJSON (RFC 7946: “a line between two positions is a straight Cartesian line”).
The polar versions are derived from this definition: each boundary is densified to 0.2° in longitude/latitude, then projected to a south polar Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area projection (+proj=laea +lat_0=-90 +lon_0=0 +datum=WGS84, equivalent to EPSG:6932). The polar version can be used directly for areas. The EPSG:3031 (polar stereographic) version is projected from the polar version, for use with Quantarctica and similar.


The anti-meridian
The West Pacific sector crosses the anti-meridian (180°), so in longitude/latitude each West Pacific region is two pieces. In version 06 each region is one row: a single polygon in the polar versions, and a two-part multipolygon in longitude/latitude. (In version 05 the pieces are separate rows: 24 rows, WP names appear twice, and measo_names is row-aligned with them.)


Coastline
The _coastline versions (R package only) have the Antarctic continent cut out. The coastline is the main continental coastline (grounding line), so ice shelves remain part of the regions and islands are not cut out.

title: Definition
text:
Colours
Each MEASO region has the colour it has in the MEASO Summary for Policymakers (Constable et al. 2023, Figure 5, “MEASO assessment areas”, adapted from McCormack et al. 2021; column fill). Each sector has its own hue, light to dark from the Antarctic to the Northern zone, so all 15 regions are distinct. The published figure uses print (CMYK) colours, so the values here are a rendering of it (made with Ghostscript): other renderings differ slightly. See Illustrations.
Version 05 had different colours: sectors that alternate around the continent shared a palette (West Pacific with Atlantic, East Pacific with Central Indian, East Indian its own), so some regions had the same colour. The West Pacific and Atlantic palette is close to the zone colours of the Summary for Policymakers (Figure 7). These are recorded in Illustrations.

title: Definition
text:
History

03 — from the original Manifold project (MEASO03.map), south to 80°S, unnamed northern region.
04 — “WestAtlantic” renamed to “Atlantic”.
05 — T regions added in the north of each sector; _coastline versions.
05.1 — extended south to 85°S; colours added. The first WPA row has a fill that doesn’t match the second (an error, kept as released).
06 — the boundaries of 05, with one row per region (the anti-meridian split dissolved), labels (“Antarctic Atlantic”), and the colours of the MEASO Summary for Policymakers. Files published as GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf and GeoJSON, with a QGIS style. Version 05 is kept as released.

title: Definition
text:
Known issues and open questions

Names are assigned by the order of polygons after polygonizing, so the build depends on that order being stable.
The south edge is 85°S: the versions without the coastline have a small hole at the pole.
In the _coastline versions the continent was cut out in longitude/latitude, closing the coastline at its southernmost latitude (about 84.4°S) rather than at the pole, so a thin band from about 84.4°S to 85°S remains in each Antarctic region (visible near the pole in the maps). This affects areas “without the continent”.
Near South America the fronts do not reach the Drake Passage sector line, so the Atlantic T region (AOT) extends south to about 55.7°S and the East Pacific T region (EPT) to about 58.9°S there.
The MEASO Summary for Policymakers describes the Northern zone as extending to the Subtropical Front “but no further north than 40°S”. Between 9°W and 10°E the (simplified) front used here reaches 38.3°S, so the Atlantic Northern region (AON) extends about 1.7° north of 40°S there (about 30 square degrees). The other sectors’ Northern regions stop at or south of 40°S.

Which to use:

Polar equal area (measo_regions06.*): areas, maps of the Southern Ocean, overlays with polar data.
Longitude/latitude (measo_regions06_ll.*): assigning regions to longitude/latitude data, web maps. Boundaries are straight in longitude/latitude (see Definition).
EPSG:3031 (measo_regions06_epsg_3031.*): polar stereographic maps, e.g. Quantarctica. Not equal area.
GeoParquet for data tools (R, Python, DuckDB, the browser); FlatGeobuf for GIS and streaming; GeoJSON for simple web maps.

GeoParquet for data tools (R, Python, DuckDB, the browser); FlatGeobuf for GIS and streaming; GeoJSON for simple web maps.

title: Data
text:
Versions
The v06 in the URL is the version of the regions. Version 06 has the boundaries of version 05, with one row per region, labels, and the published colours; see Definition and News. Version 05 is available in the R package as released (measo_regions05), and as the geopackages in inst/extdata.

title: DuckDB
text: DuckDB reads GeoParquet over HTTP, and with the spatial extension the geometry column is a GEOMETRY. The same SQL works in the DuckDB CLI, and from R, Python, or the browser. Code on this page is not run when the site is built.

title: DuckDB
DuckDB
DuckDB
text:
Assign regions to points
DuckDB spatial works in the plane, which matches the regions’ definition (boundaries straight in longitude/latitude), so longitude/latitude points are tested against measo_regions06_ll directly:
WITH pts AS (
  SELECT * FROM (VALUES (147.3, -50.2), (100.5, -60.5), (-10.5, -70.5), (-82.5, -45.5), (171.5, -65.5), (-175.5, -65.5))
    AS t(lon, lat)
)
SELECT pts.lon, pts.lat, r.name, r.sector, r.zone
FROM pts
LEFT JOIN read_parquet(getvariable('base') || '/measo_regions06_ll.parquet') AS r
  ON ST_Within(ST_Point(pts.lon, pts.lat), r.geometry)
ORDER BY ALL;
For a table of your own, replace pts with e.g. read_csv('obs.csv').
Many boundaries run along whole or half degrees of longitude and latitude, so data on a regular grid can fall exactly on a boundary. Such a point is within neither region; use ST_Intersects instead of ST_Within to get both regions (and then choose one).

title: DuckDB
text:
Areas
Use the polar equal area version:
SELECT name, round(ST_Area(geometry) / 1e6) AS area_km2
FROM read_parquet(getvariable('base') || '/measo_regions06.parquet')
ORDER BY area_km2 DESC;

title: DuckDB
text:
From R and Python
library(duckdb)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
dbExecute(con, "INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial;")
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT name, sector, zone FROM read_parquet('https://australianantarcticdivision.github.io/measoshapes/data/v06/measo_regions06_ll.parquet')")
import duckdb
duckdb.sql("INSTALL spatial; LOAD spatial;")
duckdb.sql("SELECT name, sector, zone FROM read_parquet('https://australianantarcticdivision.github.io/measoshapes/data/v06/measo_regions06_ll.parquet')")
In the browser, DuckDB-Wasm runs the same queries: see Web.

title: MEASO regions
text:
The MEASO regions divide the Southern Ocean into five sectors and three zones, giving 15 regions for assessment, summary and comparison. A fourth, northern band in each sector (the “T” regions) covers the remaining ocean to 30°S so that any location in the domain falls in exactly one region.
Figure 1: MEASO regions (version 06) in the colours of the MEASO Summary for Policymakers, with the Antarctic continent (grey) cut out. T regions (outside MEASO) are outlined only.

remotes::install_github("AustralianAntarcticDivision/measoshapes")

measo_regions06

title: MEASO regions
text:
How the regions are defined
The regions are built from lines: sector boundaries, three simplified ocean fronts, and the domain edges (85°S to 30°S, all longitudes). Their boundaries are straight lines in longitude/latitude. See Definition.

title: Python
text: The examples use geopandas. Code on this page is not run when the site is built.

title: Python
text:
Reading
GeoParquet, from a URL (needs fsspec and aiohttp) or a local file:
import geopandas as gpd

base = "https://australianantarcticdivision.github.io/measoshapes/data/v06"
regions = gpd.read_parquet(f"{base}/measo_regions06.parquet")
regions_ll = gpd.read_parquet(f"{base}/measo_regions06_ll.parquet")
regions.crs
FlatGeobuf or GeoJSON are read with GDAL (via pyogrio), which reads URLs directly:
regions = gpd.read_file(f"{base}/measo_regions06.fgb")

title: Python
text:
Assigning regions to data
geopandas works in the plane, which matches the regions’ definition (boundaries straight in longitude/latitude), so longitude/latitude points can be joined directly to measo_regions06_ll:
import pandas as pd

pts = pd.DataFrame({"lon": [147.3, 100.5, -10.5, -82.5, 171.5, -175.5],
                    "lat": [-50.2, -60.5, -70.5, -45.5, -65.5, -65.5]})
pts = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pts, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(pts.lon, pts.lat), crs="OGC:CRS84")
gpd.sjoin(pts, regions_ll, how="left", predicate="within")[["lon", "lat", "name", "label"]]
     lon   lat name         sector       zone
0  147.3 -50.2  EIN     EastIndian   Northern
1  100.5 -60.5  CIA  CentralIndian  Antarctic
2  -10.5 -70.5  AOA       Atlantic  Antarctic
3  -82.5 -45.5  EPN    EastPacific   Northern
4  171.5 -65.5  WPA    WestPacific  Antarctic
5 -175.5 -65.5  WPA    WestPacific  Antarctic
A point exactly on a boundary (common for gridded data, as many boundaries run along whole or half degrees) is within neither region; use predicate="intersects" to get both.

title: Python
text:
Areas
Use the polar equal area version:
regions.assign(area_km2=regions.area / 1e6)[["name", "area_km2"]]

title: Python
text:
Maps
The fill column has the colours:
ax = regions.plot(color=regions["fill"].fillna("#FFFFFF"),
                  edgecolor="grey", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_axis_off()

title: R
text:
Reading from a URL
No package installation is needed to read the published files. GDAL reads them directly from the URL.
u <- "https://australianantarcticdivision.github.io/measoshapes/data/v06/measo_regions06.parquet"

## sf
x <- sf::read_sf(u)

## terra
v <- terra::vect(u)

## gdalraster
lyr <- gdalraster::GDALVector$new(paste0("/vsicurl/", u))
d <- lyr$fetch(-1)
lyr$close()

## arrow, geometry as well-known binary (wk/geoarrow)
library(geoarrow)
tab <- arrow::read_parquet(u)
FlatGeobuf and GeoJSON work the same way (change the file name), and are a good choice if your GDAL doesn’t have the Parquet driver (check "Parquet" %in% sf::st_drivers()$name).

title: R
text:
Assigning regions to data
To find the region for longitude/latitude locations, transform them to the polar equal area projection and join with the polar regions:

regions <- read_sf(file.path(dd, "measo_regions06.parquet"))  ## or the URL above
pts <- data.frame(lon = c(147.3, 100.5, -10.5, -82.5, 171.5, -175.5),
                  lat = c(-50.2, -60.5, -70.5, -45.5, -65.5, -65.5))
p <- st_as_sf(pts, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = "OGC:CRS84", remove = FALSE)
p <- st_join(st_transform(p, st_crs(regions)), regions)
st_drop_geometry(p)

     lon   lat name                    label        sector      zone    fill
1  147.3 -50.2  EIN     Northern East Indian    EastIndian  Northern #878DC5
2  100.5 -60.5  CIA Antarctic Central Indian CentralIndian Antarctic #F9D7C2
3  -10.5 -70.5  AOA       Antarctic Atlantic      Atlantic Antarctic #F9BDBC
4  -82.5 -45.5  EPN    Northern East Pacific   EastPacific  Northern #4B7E7F
5  171.5 -65.5  WPA   Antarctic West Pacific   WestPacific Antarctic #E0B8D6
6 -175.5 -65.5  WPA   Antarctic West Pacific   WestPacific Antarctic #E0B8D6


The polar regions are densified to 0.2° from the longitude/latitude definition, so this agrees with the definition except for locations within a very short distance of a boundary.
For gridded data, the same applies: classify cell centres, or rasterize the polar regions onto your grid (e.g. terra::rasterize(terra::vect(regions), grid, field = "name")).
